scope_statement: A multiscale evidence-graded inventory of candidate mechanisms and interactions in Alzheimer disease. This catalogue is a research map, not a proven universal sequence, an executable causal DAG, a patient-specific model, or a source of fitted coefficients.

nodes.label: Pathogenic APP / PSEN1 / PSEN2 variants
nodes.description: Rare pathogenic variants can alter APP processing and cause autosomal-dominant Alzheimer disease with high penetrance. They provide the clearest human genetic route into amyloid biology.
limitations: This route explains a small minority of cases and must not be generalized as the sole origin of sporadic Alzheimer disease.

nodes.label: Polygenic late-onset susceptibility
nodes.description: Common and rare variants across lipid transport, endosomal trafficking and innate immune biology modify risk for late-onset Alzheimer disease.
limitations: Risk loci are not interchangeable; some signals may be pleiotropic, cell-type-specific or not directly causal.

nodes.label: Age-related loss of tissue homeostasis
nodes.description: Age-related changes in proteostasis, vascular function, immune regulation, mitochondrial quality control and repair can lower resilience to multiple pathogenic stresses.
limitations: Age is a major risk determinant, not a complete mechanistic explanation or an individually sufficient cause.

nodes.label: APOE-dependent lipid transport and clearance
nodes.description: APOE isoforms influence lipid transport, glial biology, amyloid handling and cellular responses; APOE epsilon-4 is the strongest common genetic risk allele for late-onset disease.
limitations: APOE epsilon-4 is probabilistic rather than deterministic; effects vary by sex, ancestry, age, cell type and co-pathology.

nodes.label: Life-course vascular and metabolic exposures
nodes.description: Midlife hypertension, diabetes, obesity and smoking are associated with later cognitive impairment and may affect perfusion, endothelial function and clearance.
limitations: Observational associations are confounded and do not establish that each exposure initiates Alzheimer-specific pathology.

nodes.label: Amyloidogenic APP cleavage
nodes.description: Sequential beta- and gamma-secretase cleavage of APP produces amyloid-beta peptides; inherited APP and presenilin variants can alter this pathway.
limitations: APP processing is physiological and generates multiple peptide species; total amyloid concentration alone does not capture production, aggregation, clearance or toxicity.

nodes.label: Soluble amyloid-beta oligomer stress
nodes.description: Soluble A-beta assemblies are candidate synaptotoxic and signaling-active species that can affect synaptic function, glia and tau-related pathways.
limitations: Species, conformation, assay and brain compartment matter; fluid concentration is not a direct measure of toxic synaptic exposure.

nodes.label: Parenchymal plaques and cerebral amyloid angiopathy
nodes.description: Fibrillar amyloid-beta accumulates in parenchymal plaques and vessel walls, with distinct regional, cellular and clearance contexts.
limitations: Plaque burden is not a complete proxy for oligomer toxicity, tau burden, vascular injury or clinical severity.

nodes.label: Endosomal sorting and trafficking impairment
nodes.description: Altered endosomal trafficking and recycling can perturb APP processing, receptor turnover and delivery of proteins to degradative pathways.
limitations: Human association does not by itself establish temporal primacy; cell type and subcellular compartment are critical.

nodes.label: Autophagy-lysosome clearance failure
nodes.description: Impaired autophagosome maturation, lysosomal acidification or cargo clearance can promote persistence of protein aggregates and damaged organelles.
limitations: Autophagy markers can rise when flux is blocked; static abundance must not be mistaken for effective clearance flux.

nodes.label: Ubiquitin-proteasome and chaperone overload
nodes.description: Chaperone capacity and ubiquitin-proteasome degradation participate in protein quality control and may be overwhelmed by persistent misfolded cargo.
limitations: Pathway-level evidence is heterogeneous and is not directly represented by a single protein concentration.

nodes.label: Tau phosphorylation and mislocalization
nodes.description: Abnormal tau phosphorylation, conformation and compartmentalization can impair microtubule-associated functions and increase aggregation propensity.
limitations: Tau phosphorylation is site-specific and stage-dependent; plasma p-tau biomarkers are not interchangeable with intracellular tau pathology.

nodes.label: Tau seeding and network propagation
nodes.description: Misfolded tau assemblies can seed further tau misfolding and spread along connected neural systems, contributing to the regional pattern of pathology.
limitations: In vivo human directionality, strain effects and the extent of activity-dependent spread remain incompletely resolved.

nodes.label: Microglial state dysregulation
nodes.description: Microglia can clear amyloid and debris, but persistent or context-specific states may alter inflammatory signaling, phagocytosis and tissue support.
limitations: Microglia are not a binary good/bad cell class; states change with region, age, pathology and disease stage.

nodes.label: Complement-associated synaptic elimination
nodes.description: Complement signaling and glial phagocytosis are candidate mechanisms for excessive removal of vulnerable synapses in neurodegenerative settings.
limitations: Much mechanistic evidence is preclinical; contribution and timing in human sporadic Alzheimer disease require stronger validation.

nodes.label: Astrocytic lipid and metabolic support alteration
nodes.description: Astrocytes regulate lipid transport, glucose/lactate support, glutamate handling and vascular coupling; altered support can affect neuronal resilience.
limitations: Astrocytic states are heterogeneous and can be adaptive or maladaptive; peripheral metabolic biomarkers are not direct brain measures.

nodes.label: Mitochondrial bioenergetic and quality-control failure
nodes.description: Mitochondrial changes can impair ATP production, organelle quality control, calcium handling and communication with the endoplasmic reticulum and glia.
limitations: Mitochondrial dysfunction may be cause, consequence or amplifier depending on stage and cell type.

nodes.label: Redox and calcium homeostasis failure
nodes.description: Oxidative stress, antioxidant capacity and calcium dysregulation can reinforce mitochondrial and synaptic dysfunction.
limitations: Oxidative-stress markers are highly context-dependent and are not specific proof of an initiating lesion.

nodes.label: Glucose and lipid metabolic dysregulation
nodes.description: Altered glucose utilization and lipid handling may interact with APOE, mitochondria, membrane composition and glial support across the Alzheimer continuum.
limitations: FDG-PET is a regional glucose-utilization measure, not a direct readout of mitochondrial ATP production or whole-body metabolic state.

nodes.label: Neurovascular unit and blood-brain barrier dysfunction
nodes.description: Endothelial, pericyte, astrocytic and smooth-muscle dysfunction can disturb perfusion, barrier integrity, neurovascular coupling and trophic support.
limitations: Timing and causal contribution vary across individuals; available MRI markers do not capture all microvascular pathology.

nodes.label: Perivascular and glymphatic clearance impairment
nodes.description: Altered perivascular drainage and clearance may reduce amyloid-beta elimination and interact with vascular basement membrane changes.
limitations: Mechanisms and measurement in living humans remain challenging; glymphatic claims require careful operational definitions.

nodes.label: Synaptic plasticity and circuit dysfunction
nodes.description: Synaptic failure includes altered transmission, plasticity, network activity and connectivity and is closely linked to cognitive impairment.
limitations: Clinical scales and structural MRI do not directly measure synaptic efficacy; network-level deficits may be partly compensated.

nodes.label: Axonal transport and neuritic integrity failure
nodes.description: Tau-related microtubule disruption, energetic failure and proteostatic stress can compromise axonal transport and neuritic maintenance.
limitations: Neurofilament levels indicate aspects of axonal injury but do not localize cause or quantify all forms of tissue damage.

nodes.label: Neuronal degeneration and cell loss
nodes.description: Persistent neuronal dysfunction can progress to cell loss and regional tissue atrophy, reducing the substrate available for neural computation.
limitations: Atrophy is an indirect, region-dependent measure and is affected by aging and co-pathology.

nodes.label: Persistent accumulated structural damage
nodes.description: A cumulative burden of persistent synaptic, neuritic, neuronal and neurovascular injury can retain the history of damaging exposure beyond the current stress state.
limitations: A scalar global score would hide tissue compartment and regional differences; this construct requires longitudinal operationalization.

nodes.label: Cognitive reserve and compensatory capacity
nodes.description: Reserve and network compensation can modify how much accumulated brain pathology is expressed as measurable clinical impairment.
limitations: Reserve is difficult to measure directly and may vary by domain, life history, education, network health and co-pathology.

nodes.label: Clinical cognitive and functional decline
nodes.description: Clinical decline emerges from the interaction of Alzheimer pathology, accumulated damage, regional network vulnerability, reserve and other co-pathologies.
limitations: Symptoms are downstream phenotype and must not be used as a direct measurement of a single molecular mechanism.

nodes.label: TDP-43, Lewy-body and vascular co-pathology
nodes.description: Additional proteinopathies and vascular lesions can co-occur with Alzheimer pathology and alter cognitive expression, progression and apparent response to amyloid-directed treatment.
limitations: Co-pathology prevalence, burden and regional distribution vary; detection is incomplete in living participants and does not imply a single shared origin.

edges.relationship: pathogenic_variant alters APP cleavage or gamma-secretase processing
edges.context: Autosomal-dominant familial Alzheimer disease due to APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2 variants.
limitations: Applies to rare familial forms; not a universal account of late-onset disease.

edges.relationship: susceptibility loci implicate endosomal trafficking and clearance pathways
edges.context: Late-onset Alzheimer risk architecture includes endosomal and trafficking biology.
limitations: Risk loci are heterogeneous; individual gene-to-mechanism direction requires locus-specific colocalization and functional validation.

edges.relationship: genetic susceptibility acts partly through APOE and lipid biology
edges.context: APOE is a major common genetic risk locus and influences lipid handling in brain cells.
limitations: Do not interpret APOE genotype as deterministically predicting an individual's disease or trajectory.

edges.relationship: age-related vascular and clearance changes may lower A-beta elimination
edges.context: Aging and vascular basement-membrane changes may affect perivascular clearance.
limitations: Part of the evidence is preclinical; direct causal timing in sporadic human disease is unresolved.

edges.relationship: vascular risk exposures may impair perfusion and endothelial-pericyte function
edges.context: Midlife vascular risk associates with later cognitive impairment and vascular brain injury.
limitations: Confounding and reverse causality must be addressed; not every vascular exposure is an Alzheimer-specific initiator.

edges.relationship: amyloidogenic APP processing generates A-beta species that can form soluble assemblies
edges.context: APP and presenilin genetics, biochemical assays and experimental models support an A-beta production-to-aggregation route.
limitations: Specific toxic species and the relation between fluid measures, oligomers and plaque burden are unresolved.

edges.relationship: endosomal compartment changes can alter APP trafficking and cleavage context
edges.context: Endosomal biology is genetically and mechanistically implicated in Alzheimer pathophysiology.
limitations: The direction and magnitude depend on cell type, compartment and disease stage.

edges.relationship: endosomal trafficking and lysosomal delivery are coupled clearance pathways
edges.context: Trafficking defects can alter cargo delivery and lysosomal processing.
limitations: Static marker changes cannot distinguish defective flux from compensatory upregulation.

edges.relationship: reduced clearance may increase retention and deposition of amyloid-beta
edges.context: Perivascular clearance impairment is a candidate contributor to amyloid accumulation and CAA.
limitations: Human causal ordering and in-vivo clearance quantification remain uncertain.

edges.relationship: A-beta and tau pathophysiology interact through signaling and cellular stress pathways
edges.context: Current models support interaction between A-beta and tau processes, not a simple one-way chain in every subject.
limitations: Temporal precedence and causal strength vary across models and human disease subtypes.

edges.relationship: misprocessed tau can seed and propagate conformational pathology
edges.context: Tau aggregation and regional spread are supported by neuropathological, imaging and experimental work.
limitations: Human in-vivo transfer mechanisms and strain specificity remain active research questions.

edges.relationship: amyloid species alter microglial sensing, phagocytosis and inflammatory state
edges.context: A-beta and innate immune systems interact at plaque and tissue interfaces.
limitations: Microglial responses are heterogeneous and may be protective or harmful by context.

edges.relationship: microglial immune state can alter complement-mediated synapse tagging and removal
edges.context: Complement and glial phagocytosis are candidate routes to synaptic loss.
limitations: Causal role and timing in human late-onset disease need further validation.

edges.relationship: excessive synaptic elimination can reduce synaptic substrate and circuit function
edges.context: Synapse elimination is one plausible mechanism connecting immune activity to circuit dysfunction.
limitations: Not all synaptic loss is complement-mediated; regional and stage effects matter.

edges.relationship: reduced degradative flux may contribute to persistence of abnormal tau species
edges.context: Autophagy-lysosome systems participate in clearance of protein and organelle cargo.
limitations: The relationship can be bidirectional; static measurements cannot establish flux or direction.

edges.relationship: overloaded protein quality-control systems may increase persistence of misfolded tau
edges.context: Protein quality control interacts with tau biology and general proteotoxic stress.
limitations: This is a candidate mechanism, not a calibrated or universally demonstrated human causal edge.

edges.relationship: APOE isoform and lipidation state can modify cellular trafficking and amyloid handling
edges.context: APOE links genetic risk, lipid transport, glial responses and amyloid handling.
limitations: Do not reduce the pleiotropic APOE effects to one endosomal pathway.

edges.relationship: altered astrocytic substrate and lipid support may worsen neuronal energy stress
edges.context: Astrocyte-neuron metabolic coupling is a plausible bridge between systemic metabolism and neuronal vulnerability.
limitations: Human directionality and effect size are not established; cell-specific data are needed.

edges.relationship: substrate and lipid dysregulation can alter mitochondrial energy metabolism
edges.context: Metabolic and mitochondrial pathways interact across the Alzheimer continuum.
limitations: Metabolic dysfunction may be upstream, downstream or mutually reinforcing by stage.

edges.relationship: mitochondrial stress can disturb redox and calcium homeostasis
edges.context: Mitochondrial energy and quality-control defects interact with redox and calcium pathways.
limitations: Bidirectional feedback and cell-type specificity prevent a single fixed direction.

edges.relationship: redox and calcium disturbances can impair synaptic signaling and plasticity
edges.context: Oxidative and calcium stress are linked to synaptic dysfunction in mechanistic models.
limitations: Oxidative markers are nonspecific and may represent consequence as well as cause.

edges.relationship: vascular and pericyte dysfunction may impair perivascular drainage and amyloid clearance
edges.context: Pericyte, endothelial and basement-membrane changes interact with perfusion and clearance.
limitations: Not all clearance routes are equally measurable in living humans.

edges.relationship: vascular injury may affect amyloid retention and cerebral amyloid angiopathy
edges.context: Vascular and amyloid pathology can reinforce each other, including CAA-associated vascular injury.
limitations: Directionality may differ between parenchymal plaques and vascular amyloid.

edges.relationship: regional tau pathology is associated with synaptic and circuit dysfunction
edges.context: Tau burden and topography track neuronal injury and clinical progression more closely than plaque burden in many cohorts.
limitations: Association does not fully establish molecular mediation or an identical route in every subtype.

edges.relationship: persistent synaptic structural loss contributes to cumulative tissue injury burden
edges.context: A cumulative damage compartment can represent persistent loss that is not identical to current synaptic stress.
limitations: Requires operational definitions and longitudinal measurement; must not double-count synaptic markers.

edges.relationship: sustained neuritic and axonal injury contributes to persistent damage
edges.context: Axonal injury markers and regional tissue loss support persistent injury processes.
limitations: NfL is not a direct measure of irreversible axon loss and is not disease-specific.

edges.relationship: neuronal cell loss contributes directly to persistent accumulated tissue damage
edges.context: Neuronal loss and atrophy are persistent structural consequences of neurodegeneration.
limitations: In-vivo imaging measures are indirect and should carry regional uncertainty.

edges.relationship: persistent damage reduces available neural substrate and contributes to functional decline
edges.context: Accumulated neuropathologic and vascular burden relates to clinical expression and functional outcomes.
limitations: The mapping is nonlinear and modified by regional distribution, reserve and co-pathology.

edges.relationship: reserve and compensation can buffer or delay clinical expression of brain pathology
edges.context: Biological and clinical staging are distinct; reserve and resistance modify their relationship.
limitations: Reserve is latent, multidimensional and difficult to separate from education, baseline ability and life-course factors.

edges.relationship: co-pathologies can add to or interact with Alzheimer pathology in shaping clinical decline
edges.context: Co-pathologies contribute to cognitive variability, progression and treatment-response heterogeneity.
limitations: This edge represents effect modification and additive/mixed pathology, not a single common causal chain.
